article.title: Transnational Prosecutions
article.author: Ann Garrison
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At 7 pm on Saturday, November 7th, ICE agents appeared at the Plymouth Correctional Facility in Plymouth, Massachusetts, and handcuffed prisoner Jean Léonard Teganya. No one knew of his whereabouts after that until Monday, November 9 when his family in Canada and the US learned that he was in Kigali, Rwanda, deported even though his appeal of a deportation order was still pending. The essentials of his case are, as I have described them here before: A Rwandan refugee of Hutu ethnicity is charged with genocide crime decades after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Witnesses in Rwanda make accusations that they have for some reason kept to themselves for decades. No hard evidence is produced. A jury convicts the accused because they are a Hutu and all Hutus are assumed to be guilty of genocide crime. Although the jurors may give other reasons, they believe that Hutus were the only killers in Rwanda in 1994, that they massacred 800,000 or a million innocent Tutsis and “moderate Hutus,” so this Hutu defendant must be guilty like all the others. Related: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize and the Dark Legacy of the Rwanda Tribunal The accused then serves time in an American prison for hiding his guilt of genocide crime on his immigration papers. Upon release, he or she faces deportation to stand trial for genocide crimes in Rwanda, where they are convicted and sentenced, usually to life in prison. The Rwandan press is all controlled by President Paul Kagame’s totalitarian regime. The central narrative that it constantly repeats is that only Hutus committed crimes during Rwanda’s 1990-1994 war and during the massacres of its final 100 days. This narrative is even legally enforced; anyone who differs can go to prison for the crime of “genocide denial” in Rwanda. When social scientists Christian Davenport and Allan Stamm went to Rwanda to study the war and genocide, they quickly concluded that something was wrong with the story because everyone recited it as though by rote, exactly the same, without variation, as Allen Stam explained in his University of Michigan lecture “ Understanding the Rwandan Genocide .” This story of Tutsi innocence and Hutu guilt was spread worldwide by the hugely persuasive Hollywood movie Hotel Rwanda. It was institutionalized by the International Criminal Tribunal on Rwanda, which never indicted a single Tutsi, including the one who most deserved indictment—then General, now President Paul Kagame. Kagame’s own Chief of Staff, General Kayumba Nyamwasa told the BBC, in Rwanda’s Untold Story , that he ordered soldiers to assassinate Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira by shooting their plane out of the sky over Kigali on April 6, 1994. Those assassinations panicked the population, including the million IDPs in camps encircling Kigali after four years of civil war, and triggered the infamous massacres known as the genocide. Related: Ethiopia vs. Eritrea: A New War Could Send Oil and Gas Prices Soaring It has also been proven, by author Judi Rever and others, that as many or more Hutus died during the war and genocide, and that Kagame’s troops had infiltrated the Interahamwe, the government’s youth militia, and then egged them on during the killing to engineer the genocide that later gave him a specious excuse to rule. After seizing power, Kagame claimed to be the hero who had ended the genocide when in fact he started it, and Western leaders, most notably Bill Cinton and Tony Blair, reinforce that claim to this day. In 2009, in a particularly Orwellian moment, Bill Clinton presented Kagame with a Gloobal Citizen Award for Leadership in Public Service. Even this, however, is not enough. In order to remain in power, the Kagame regime must make sure that Rwandans in diaspora are constantly afraid, fearful of speaking out against the Rwandan government’s domestic repression or its 30+ years of war and resource plunder in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These prosecutions and deportations are central to maintaining that climate of fear and Western governments, including the US, have been more than willing to collaborate. The mining and industrial interests they represent have benefited hugely from the resource plunder, all according to plan, and as documented in decades of UN reports . No innocence presumed As soon as Jean Léonard Teganya arrived in Rwanda, Kagame’s most prominent media vehicle, the New Times of Rwanda, ran the headline “ Minister Bizimana on US-deported Teganya: 'He was a cruel killer and rapist'. ” Jean-Damascène Bizimana is, laughably, the Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement. Why bother to stage a trial without presumed innocence, the first principle of criminal law? Because for years, the West has expected Kagame to stage such trials just as he stages elections, the last of which he “won” by 98.2% . Related: Trump Amps Up Anti-Ilhan, anti-Somali Hysteria On November 10, Aljazeera published what they call an “Explainer” headlined “ Who is Jean Léonard Teganya, deported by US over Rwanda genocide claims? ” It said: "He [Jean Léonard] applied for asylum in Canada, but his application was rejected in 2002 and again in 2012. The Canadian authorities’ decision, as described in the US appeal judgement, was based on the conclusion that he would not have survived in Rwanda in 1994 if he had not been perceived as sharing the intention to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.” This is more of the non-stop illogic of Rwanda’s totalitarian narrative, which most of the world has accepted since 1994. By that measure, every single Hutu who survived the genocide must have “shared the intent to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.” How then could any of the famous “moderate Hutu” have survived? Next in the Dock: Eric Tabaro Nshimiye Any Rwandan who dares to testify on behalf of another in one of these trials is likely to find themselves accused, indicted, prosecuted, deported, and imprisoned in time as well. Eric Tabaro Nshimiye testified on behalf of Jean Léonard Teganya in 2019, and on October 26, 2016, a jury found him guilty of lying on his immigration papers and lying on behalf of Jean Léonard. Eric and Jean Léonard were both medical students at the University of Rwanda’s teaching hospital in Butare in 1994, at the time of the massacres. Seven years ago, after Eric testified on Jean Léonard’s behalf, a criminal defense attorney urged him to leave the US, to find another home and establish another identity wherever he could because there was no doubt that he would be next and no chance he would receive a fair trial. But Eric didn’t run. He has work, family, faith, and community here. For more than two decades, he has worked for Goodyear Tire and Rubber as an electrical engineer while living in Lake Township, in the Uniontown, Ohio area. In March 2024, he was arrested and charged with crimes like those Jean Léonard and so many others have been charged with. In the Ohio District Court, seventy friends and family members, including even his dentist, submitted statements to say that he is a devoted husband and father and an upstanding, engaged member of his community and church. Friends and family traveled from all over the US and even Canada for his detention hearing in Youngstown. They stood outside with signs reading, “Eric Is a Man of Virtue,” “Eric Is a Man of High Morals,” “Eric Is a Man of Faith,” and more. As reported by the Canton Repository , “they huddled in prayer, hugged, shook hands and shed a few tears.” They have no doubt seen this pattern play out many times before. I traveled to Boston for Eric’s arraignment in federal court, where family filled all the benches in a small courtroom, then offered up the equity in their homes as bail, hoping to secure his release while awaiting trial. Sadly, they failed and on October 26, 2026, Eric was convicted. He now awaits sentencing on January 26 next year. Related: Trump Amps Up Anti-Ilhan, anti-Somali Hysteria In the backdrop of Eric and Jean Léonard’s tragedies is that of political prisoner Victoire Ingabire Umuhoza, who left a very successful, settled life in the Netherlands in 2010 to return to Rwanda and challenge Paul Kagame in that year’s presidential election. She went to prison for the “crime” instead. Perhaps even more importantly, she was convicted of “genocide denial,” of challenging the singular narrative that only Hutus committed crimes during Rwanda’s war and genocide, that only Hutus, and even their children, will pay for them now and forever. She left the Netherlands knowing that she would likely be assassinated or imprisoned but urging her followers to pick up where she left off. Kagame had Victoire arrested again in June 2025, on charges like fomenting civil unrest and encouraging members of her party to read a book on nonviolent protest. The charges have since been enhanced and this time the prosecution is seeking a life sentence. Rwandan political prisoner Victoire Ingabire's case will resume in Kigali on December 8th. The Prosecutor is seeking a life sentence. In a recent letter to her supporters, she wrote: I am in good spirits, but I am also worried for my life. The recent death of government critic Aimable Karasira in a Rwandan prison on the day he was due for release affirms my worries. I wonder whether I will ever see my family again or even speak to my children and grandchildren. But I am grateful for everyone who has spoken out for me and called for my release. Only a little of what happens outside these prison walls reaches me, but I know I have not been forgotten and I am thankful for that. I appeal to all individuals, institutions, and states that believe in democracy to join me in calling for the Rwandan regime to reform - for the greater good of its citizens and the entire region. I believe in a better future for Rwanda, but it cannot be built while independent voices are silenced." Sadly, this persecution feels neither new nor surprising. Despite what the charges state, my crime is being a woman who is not afraid to dream out loud of a better future for Rwanda. My requests to speak to my children have been refused since my arrest in June 2025. I have only occasionally spoken briefly to my gravely ill husband. There are times when prison guards confiscated my documents and those of my lawyers, thereby interfering with our preparations for my defense. I have been prevented from meeting with my co-accused to prepare my defense and barred from attending worship services within the prison, an opportunity granted to the other inmates. I have been a person of deep faith my entire life. In my darkest moments, I draw great strength from my faith. I believe that by taking away even my right to spiritual nourishment during my imprisonment, the regime is trying to break my will. What they don't understand is that when you know your cause is just, nothing can break you. Black Agenda Report
